Title: AIR Demonstrates Vulnerability in Skill Scanning with Fake AI Agent Skill

Victim.Description: The victims were AI agents, including those on corporate accounts, that installed the fake skill.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involved AIR creating a fake AI agent skill to demonstrate vulnerabilities in skill scanning tools. The adversary, AIR, used the capability of developing a fake skill that bypassed security scanners. The infrastructure included a domain controlled by AIR to host the fake skill's setup instructions. The victims were AI agents, including those on corporate accounts, that installed the fake skill.
doc_summary: Security firm AIR conducted an experiment by creating a fake AI agent skill named brand-landingpage, which was pushed through a popular skill marketplace and advertised on Instagram. The skill reached approximately 26,000 agents, including some on corporate accounts. Despite being marked safe by every skill security scanner tested, the payload was designed to be harmless, collecting only the user's email address. The experiment highlighted the inadequacy of current trust signals, such as GitHub stars and clean scanner verdicts, in detecting malicious skills. The skill initially pointed to genuine documentation but later redirected to a page instructing agents to download and run a script. This demonstrated the structural problem of skill scanning tools, which only check a fixed package and not the external links that can be altered post-review. The incident underscores the need for treating skills as software, vetting external links, and maintaining control over skill installations.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain stages involved reconnaissance by identifying trust signals and scanner limitations, weaponization by developing a fake skill, delivery through a skill marketplace and Instagram ads, exploitation of trust in GitHub stars and clean scanner verdicts, installation by agents, command and control through a redirected page, and actions on objectives by collecting email addresses.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes domain names as the primary indicator, with stitch-design.ai being used to host the fake skill's setup instructions. The incident highlights the challenge of detecting malicious activities when external links can be altered post-review. The scoring reflects the difficulty in addressing domain-based indicators.

Title: Scattered Spider Cyberattack on Transport for London

Victim.Description: Transport for London, a key part of the UK's critical national infrastructure.

diamond_model_summary: The Scattered Spider cybercrime group targeted Transport for London (TfL) in a significant cyberattack, causing operational disruptions and financial losses. The attackers used Telegram for communication and accessed TfL's Oyster refunds system, impacting critical infrastructure. The National Crime Agency led the investigation, uncovering evidence of the group's activities. The attack highlights the importance of securing critical infrastructure and engaging with law enforcement early in such incidents.
doc_summary: In 2024, the Scattered Spider cybercrime group, including members Thalha Jubair and Owen Flowers, executed a cyberattack on Transport for London (TfL), causing significant financial damage and operational disruptions. The attack targeted TfL's Oyster refunds system, delaying customer refunds and affecting critical national infrastructure. The National Crime Agency (NCA) led the investigation, uncovering evidence of the group's activities, including screenshots and videos of the breach. The attackers communicated via Telegram and an online collaboration platform. The incident resulted in £29 million in losses and forced TfL employees to visit local offices. The group was also linked to breaches in the healthcare sector, specifically SSM Health Care Corporation and Sutter Health. The guilty plea was entered at Woolwich Crown Court, with sentencing scheduled for July 16, 2024.
kill_chain_summary: The attack on TfL by the Scattered Spider group followed a structured kill chain. The attackers likely conducted reconnaissance to gather information on TfL's systems. They exploited vulnerabilities to gain initial access using valid accounts. Command and control were established via Telegram, and the attackers executed actions on objectives by disrupting the Oyster refunds system. The incident underscores the need for robust detection and remediation strategies across all stages of the kill chain.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for the TfL cyberattack includes various indicators. The attackers used Telegram for command and control, which is a tool that can be monitored and blocked. The use of valid accounts for initial access highlights the importance of monitoring login attempts and enforcing strong authentication measures. The disruption of the Oyster refunds system represents a significant impact on operations, emphasizing the need for robust data protection and recovery strategies.

Title: LastPass Data Breach via Klue Supply Chain Attack

Victim.Description: LastPass, a password management platform, was the primary victim, with customer data exposed.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves the Icarus group exploiting compromised credentials to access OAuth tokens, targeting LastPass's Salesforce environment. The attackers' capability to exfiltrate CRM data and launch an extortion campaign highlights the risks associated with third-party integrations. The victim, LastPass, experienced a high-severity breach, emphasizing the need for robust security measures.
doc_summary: LastPass experienced a data breach when hackers accessed customer data from its Salesforce environment by stealing OAuth tokens in a supply chain attack involving Klue. The attack, attributed to the Icarus group, involved compromising Klue's infrastructure using legacy credentials, leading to the theft of OAuth tokens. These tokens were used to access LastPass customer data, although no Gong-related data was compromised. The breach exposed CRM data, prompting LastPass to disable employee access to Klue, rotate API/OAuth tokens, and notify law enforcement. The attackers used domains like baccarat.com.au and robinskitchen.com.au for phishing. The incident highlights the risks of OAuth token theft and the importance of securing third-party integrations.
kill_chain_summary: The attack began with reconnaissance on Klue's infrastructure, followed by exploitation of compromised credentials to access OAuth tokens. The attackers then exfiltrated CRM data from LastPass's Salesforce environment, culminating in an extortion campaign. The incident underscores the importance of securing third-party integrations and monitoring for unauthorized access.

Title: Malicious npm Packages Deliver Windows RAT

Victim.Description: Developers using npm packages were targeted.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a North Korean adversary using malicious npm packages to deliver a Windows-based RAT. The adversary's capability includes using JavaScript droppers and PowerShell scripts to deploy the RAT, which communicates with a C2 server. The infrastructure involves domains and IPs for payload delivery and C2 communication. Victims are developers using npm packages, with a high impact severity due to credential theft and data exfiltration.
doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers discovered malicious npm packages designed to deliver a Windows-based remote access trojan (RAT). The packages, published by an npm user named 'abdrizak', include 'Aes-decode-runner-pro', 'postcss-minify-selector-parser', and 'postcss-minify-selector'. These packages deploy a JavaScript dropper that writes a PowerShell script to disk, which downloads a payload from 'nvidiadriver[.]net'. The payload includes a Visual Basic Script and a Python runtime, which set up the environment for the RAT. The RAT gathers host information, siphons credentials from Google Chrome, and communicates with a C2 server at '95.216.92[.]207:8080'. This attack coincides with other campaigns targeting the npm ecosystem and overlaps with a North Korean operation dubbed PolinRider, which injects obfuscated JavaScript into GitHub repositories to deliver malware.
kill_chain_summary: The attack follows a structured kill chain: reconnaissance to identify npm packages, weaponization by creating malicious packages, delivery through npm, installation of the RAT via PowerShell scripts, command and control through a C2 server, and actions on objectives including credential theft and data exfiltration. The adversary's use of legitimate tools and obfuscation techniques complicates detection and remediation efforts.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes IP addresses and domain names used for C2 communication, as well as tools like PowerShell and Visual Basic scripts. The adversary's use of legitimate technologies and obfuscation techniques increases the difficulty of detection and response. The RAT's capabilities for credential theft and data exfiltration pose significant challenges for defenders.

doc_summary: An ongoing malware campaign is targeting WhatsApp users in multiple countries with deceptive messages that push VBScript files, leading to remote system access. The threat actor uses file names indicating business and financial documents delivered by compromised contacts. By downloading and executing the malicious attachments, the infection chain installs ManageEngine Endpoint Central, used by IT administrators to manage systems. The campaign spreads across Brazil, India, Mexico, Singapore, the United Kingdom, Spain, Taiwan, Australia, Russia, Vietnam, and Malaysia. doc_summary: A vulnerability named Squidbleed (CVE-2026-47729) was discovered in the Squid web proxy, allowing a heap over-read that can leak cleartext HTTP requests, including credentials, to an attacker with proxy access. The bug originates from a 1997 FTP-parsing change and affects Squid's default configuration. The vulnerability is exploitable by a trusted client on shared networks like schools and offices. The attacker needs to control an FTP server on port 21, which is enabled by default. The issue lies in Squid's FTP directory-listing parser, where a loop fails to terminate correctly, leading to memory leakage. Researchers at Calif.io disclosed the vulnerability in June 2023, and proof-of-concept code is available. The recommended mitigation is to disable FTP in Squid configurations. The vulnerability is rated medium severity with a CVSS score of 6.5, as it requires low privileges and impacts confidentiality only.
kill_chain_summary: The Squidbleed vulnerability follows a structured kill chain, starting with reconnaissance to identify vulnerable Squid proxies. The attacker then weaponizes by setting up an FTP server to exploit the vulnerability. Delivery involves using the FTP server to deliver the exploit to the Squid proxy. Title: CastleStealer Campaign via OXLOADER and Malicious Google Ads

Victim.Description: Targets are users outside the CIS region searching for 'lts version of node.js'.

diamond_model_summary: The REF8372 campaign involves a Russian-speaking threat actor using OXLOADER to deliver CastleStealer via malicious Google Ads. The infrastructure includes fake websites and abuse of the Storj platform. Victims are targeted through misleading ads, with a focus on non-CIS regions. The campaign employs advanced obfuscation and evasion techniques, indicating a high level of sophistication.
doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed a new campaign delivering CastleStealer via OXLOADER. Elastic Security Labs identified the campaign leveraging malicious Google Ads to distribute malware. The threat actor is likely Russian-speaking and financially motivated, avoiding CIS regions. The campaign, codenamed REF8372, uses obfuscation, self-modifying decryption, and Windows .reloc section abuse. Users searching for 'lts version of node.js' are redirected to a fake site, node-js.prentiva99.info, via ads under the name 'ВОЛОДИМИР ТЕРЕЩЕНКО'. The site serves a batch script hosted on Storj, downloading OXLOADER through PowerShell. The attack uses DLL side-loading to execute CastleStealer. OXLOADER employs control-flow flattening and mixed Boolean-Arithmetic to evade detection. CastleStealer, a .NET information stealer, was distributed with CastleLoader in a campaign called BackgroundFix. OXLOADER's engineering suggests it is in an early operational phase, with low detection rates.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with reconnaissance using Google Ads to identify potential victims. Weaponization involves preparing OXLOADER with obfuscation techniques. Delivery is achieved through malicious ads redirecting to a fake website. Exploitation occurs when users run a batch script downloading OXLOADER. Installation uses DLL side-loading to execute CastleStealer. Command and Control is established via web protocols, and Actions on Objectives involve data exfiltration.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes domain names like node-js.prentiva99.info and tools such as OXLOADER. The campaign's use of advanced obfuscation techniques and legitimate services like Storj complicates detection and response efforts. The threat actor's sophisticated methods and infrastructure choices reflect deliberate efforts to evade analysis and maintain operational effectiveness.

doc_summary: Canada's spy service, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS), obtained a judge's permission to neutralize two foreign-run botnets operating on Canadian soil. The Federal Court released a public version of the ruling on June 15, 2024. This operation marked the first use of CSIS's threat reduction warrant powers to alter, degrade, and destroy botnet data on infected machines, including Canada-based servers, SOHO routers, and IoT devices. The warrant was granted by Justice Catherine Kane on May 1, 2024, and renewed in August 2024. The operation targeted devices, not individuals, and aimed to prevent foreign adversaries from using Canadian infrastructure to probe critical sectors like energy. The ruling does not specify the adversaries' identities, but the timing aligns with similar U.S. operations against Chinese and Russian state actors. The operation highlights the vulnerabilities of neglected consumer gear and the need for device owners to maintain security.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain stages include reconnaissance to identify vulnerable devices, exploitation of these devices for initial access, installation of botnet malware for persistence, and command and control operations. diamond_model_summary: AryStinger is a sophisticated malware campaign targeting outdated routers and NAS devices to create a distributed reconnaissance network. The adversary exploits known vulnerabilities in Realtek RTL819X-based routers and QNAP NAS devices, using them for internet scanning and traffic tunneling. The infrastructure includes compromised devices communicating with C2 servers over HTTP/HTTPS. The campaign primarily affects devices in South Korea and China, with a significant portion of infections in D-Link DIR-850L routers. The adversary remains unidentified, but the strategic use of forgotten hardware and ancient CVEs suggests a high level of sophistication.
doc_summary: AryStinger is a new malware family identified by QiAnXin's XLab, targeting forgotten home routers and QNAP NAS boxes. It exploits vulnerabilities CVE-2013-3307 in Linksys and CVE-2016-5681 in D-Link routers, as well as CVE-2025-11837 in QNAP NAS. The malware turns these devices into a distributed reconnaissance and proxy network, scanning the internet, fingerprinting services, and tunneling traffic. The campaign primarily affects routers with Realtek RTL819X chips, with a significant number of infections in South Korea and China. The malware uses a Dropbear SSH server for persistence and communicates with its C2 over HTTP/HTTPS. The attack was first observed on March 12, 2026, spreading from IP 107.150.106.14. The malware's infrastructure includes domains like ajb8.com, and it employs tools such as fscan, ksubdomain, and httpx for reconnaissance.
kill_chain_summary: The AryStinger campaign follows a structured kill chain, beginning with reconnaissance through internet scanning and service fingerprinting. Exploitation occurs via known vulnerabilities in outdated routers and NAS devices, leading to the installation of malware for persistence. Command and control is established through HTTP/HTTPS communication with C2 servers, using obfuscated traffic. The final stage involves actions on objectives, where compromised devices are used for footprinting and traffic tunneling. The campaign demonstrates a strategic use of outdated hardware and vulnerabilities to establish a distributed reconnaissance network.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The AryStinger campaign presents several indicators across the Pyramid of Pain. IP addresses like 107.150.106.14 and domains such as ajb8.com are used for C2 communication. The malware employs tools like fscan, ksubdomain, and httpx for reconnaissance. Known vulnerabilities CVE-2013-3307, CVE-2016-5681, and CVE-2025-11837 are exploited for initial access. The use of Protobuf-encoded traffic obfuscated by XOR adds complexity to detection efforts. The campaign's reliance on outdated hardware and vulnerabilities highlights the importance of maintaining up-to-date security measures.

Title: Prinz Eugen Ransomware Attack Analysis

Victim.Description: Organizations targeted by Prinz Eugen ransomware.

diamond_model_summary: The Prinz Eugen ransomware group employs hands-on-keyboard tactics, using legitimate RMM tools and living-off-the-land techniques to maximize impact on business-critical files. They gain initial access through stolen RDP credentials and maintain persistence with backdoor accounts. Their operations do not follow the ransomware-as-a-service model, and they avoid leaving ransom notes to reduce forensic footprints.
doc_summary: Prinz Eugen ransomware operation prioritizes recently modified files for encryption without leaving a ransom note. Threatdown, Malwarebytes' enterprise cybersecurity arm, discovered that the hackers use legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software and living-off-the-land tools. Initial access is likely through stolen RDP credentials, followed by manual download and execution of 'servertool.exe'. The attack uses RemotePC RMM tool and a backdoor administrator account for persistence. Prinz Eugen does not operate under the ransomware-as-a-service model. The ransomware employs ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption with a 32-byte master key, Argon2id, SHA-256, and HKDF-SHA256 for key derivation. The encryption process is carried out in 1 MB chunks, and file integrity is checked using SHA-256. The malware overwrites the encryption key with zeroes and self-deletes to prevent retrieval. No ransom note is dropped, reducing forensic footprint. The attack lists three victims on a data leak site, with more organizations impacted.
kill_chain_summary: The Prinz Eugen ransomware attack begins with gaining access through stolen RDP credentials, followed by the installation of 'servertool.exe' for ransomware execution. The attackers use legitimate RMM tools and backdoor accounts for persistence. The ransomware encrypts recently modified files using ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption, prioritizing business-critical data to pressure victims into paying the ransom. The absence of a ransom note complicates detection of the extortion phase.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for the Prinz Eugen ransomware attack includes the use of specific tools like RemotePC and servertool.exe, as well as TTPs such as living-off-the-land techniques and data encryption for impact. The attackers' use of legitimate tools and advanced encryption methods increases the difficulty of detection and response. The absence of specific IP addresses, domains, or hashes in the available data limits the ability to track and block the attack effectively.

Title: Mastra AI Supply Chain Attack by Sapphire Sleet

Victim.Description: Developers and organizations using compromised npm packages.

diamond_model_summary: The Mastra AI supply chain attack attributed to Sapphire Sleet involved compromising npm packages to deploy malware. The adversary, a North Korean state-sponsored group, targeted the financial sector to steal credentials and cryptocurrency. The attack leveraged malicious npm updates, a cross-platform information stealer, and C2 infrastructure.
doc_summary: Microsoft has attributed a recent supply chain attack on Mastra AI, compromising over 140 npm packages, to the North Korean hacking group Sapphire Sleet, also known as BlueNoroff. The attack involved hijacking an npm maintainer account to publish malicious package updates, injecting a dependency named 'easy-day-js', a typosquat of the legitimate dayjs library. The malicious dependency executed a post-install hook deploying a malware dropper aimed at stealing sensitive credentials, API keys, authentication tokens, and cryptocurrency wallets. The second-stage payload was a cross-platform information stealer targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS systems, collecting host information, browser histories, installed applications, and checking for cryptocurrency wallet extensions. Persistence methods varied by OS, including Windows Registry Run keys, macOS LaunchAgents, and Linux systemd services. Follow-on activity included a PowerShell backdoor, additional persistence mechanisms, and a malicious Windows service granting SYSTEM privileges. Sapphire Sleet is known for targeting the financial sector with software supply chain compromises.
kill_chain_summary: The attack began with the compromise of an npm maintainer account, leading to the weaponization of a malicious dependency. Delivery occurred through npm package updates, exploiting the supply chain. Installation involved a malware dropper, followed by C2 communication. Actions on objectives included data collection and credential theft.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes TTPs such as supply chain compromise and credential theft. Tools like a PowerShell backdoor and persistence mechanisms were used. No specific hashes, IPs, or domains were identified, limiting the ability to disrupt the adversary's operations through traditional indicators.

Title: Exploitation of CVE-2026-4020 in Gravity SMTP Plugin

Victim.Description: WordPress sites using vulnerable Gravity SMTP plugin

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves threat actors exploiting CVE-2026-4020 in the Gravity SMTP plugin, affecting WordPress sites globally. The adversary's capability includes exploiting a REST API endpoint to extract sensitive data. The infrastructure involves unauthenticated HTTP GET requests to the vulnerable endpoint. Victims are WordPress sites using the vulnerable plugin, with data types at risk including configuration data and API keys.
doc_summary: Threat actors are exploiting a medium-severity vulnerability, CVE-2026-4020, in the Gravity SMTP WordPress plugin, affecting approximately 100,000 sites. This flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to extract sensitive data, including configuration data, API keys, secrets, and OAuth tokens, via a REST API endpoint. The vulnerability is due to a permission_callback that returns true, enabling access to the endpoint. Attackers can leverage this to harvest credentials and gain insights into the site's software stack, facilitating further attacks. A patch has been released in version 2.1.5 of the plugin. Wordfence has blocked over 17 million exploit attempts, with activity peaking in early June 2026. Site owners are advised to update the plugin, rotate credentials, and review server logs for suspicious activity.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with reconnaissance to identify vulnerable WordPress sites using the Gravity SMTP plugin. Exploitation occurs through CVE-2026-4020, allowing attackers to extract sensitive data via a REST API endpoint. Actions on objectives include harvesting credentials and planning further attacks. Detection involves monitoring for specific HTTP GET requests, and remediation includes updating the plugin and rotating credentials.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes IP addresses and TTPs. IP addresses are involved in the exploit attempts, while TTPs include exploiting a public-facing application vulnerability. The lack of specific hash values, domain names, and tools limits the pyramid's complexity. Monitoring HTTP GET requests and updating the plugin are key to mitigating the threat.

doc_summary: Klue, a market intelligence platform, confirmed a security incident involving the theft of OAuth tokens by the Icarus extortion group. The attackers accessed Salesforce environments through compromised Klue Battlecards integrations, leading to data theft from multiple organizations. Klue CEO Jason Smith stated the breach was discovered on June 12, involving unauthorized access via a legacy credential. The company revoked affected credentials, removed unauthorized code, and engaged CrowdStrike for response. ReliaQuest and Huntress identified the use of Python scripts to query Salesforce's API. The stolen data included business contacts and sales communications. Icarus publicly claimed responsibility, pressuring victims to contact them via Session messaging to prevent data leaks. The incident primarily affected third-party integrations, not Klue's platform directly. Organizations warned of potential phishing and extortion risks.
kill_chain_summary: The attack began with reconnaissance on Klue's integration infrastructure, followed by exploitation of compromised OAuth tokens to access Salesforce environments. Title: usbliter8 Exploit Targets Apple's A12 and A13 SecureROM

Victim.Description: Devices with A12 and A13 chips are vulnerable.
Victim.Security_Posture: Vulnerable due to unpatchable hardware flaw

diamond_model_summary: The usbliter8 exploit, developed by Paradigm Shift, targets Apple's A12 and A13 chips by exploiting a hardware flaw in the Synopsys DWC2 USB controller. The exploit requires physical access to the device in DFU mode and uses a specific microcontroller board to execute arbitrary code in SecureROM. Devices such as iPhone XS, iPhone 11, and Apple Watch Series 4 are affected. The vulnerability is unpatchable via software updates, making affected devices permanently vulnerable. The exploit was publicly disclosed on June 18, 2026, following coordinated disclosure with Apple.
doc_summary: Security researchers at Paradigm Shift have disclosed a working exploit named usbliter8 that allows arbitrary code execution in the SecureROM of Apple's A12 and A13 chips. This exploit requires physical access to the device, which must be in DFU mode and connected via USB to a specific microcontroller board. The vulnerability stems from a hardware flaw in the Synopsys DWC2 USB controller, which allows a buffer underflow to overwrite arbitrary SRAM due to Apple's configuration of the USB DART in SecureROM. The exploit affects devices such as iPhone XS, iPhone 11, iPad Air 3rd gen, and Apple Watch Series 4 and 5. The exploit cannot be patched via software updates, making affected devices permanently vulnerable. The public proof of concept was released on June 18, 2026, following coordinated disclosure with Apple. No CVE or CVSS score has been issued, and no in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. The practical risk is low for most users, but high-security environments should consider hardware refreshes to A14 or newer.
kill_chain_summary: The usbliter8 exploit follows a specific kill chain involving physical access to the target device, exploitation of a hardware flaw in the Synopsys DWC2 USB controller, and execution of arbitrary code in SecureROM. The exploit requires the device to be in DFU mode and connected to a specific microcontroller board. The vulnerability affects Apple's A12 and A13 chips, making devices such as iPhone XS and iPhone 11 permanently vulnerable. The exploit cannot be patched via software updates, posing a high risk to affected devices.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The usbliter8 exploit presents a significant challenge in terms of detection and mitigation due to its reliance on a hardware flaw in the Synopsys DWC2 USB controller. The exploit requires physical access to the device and specific hardware setup, making traditional detection methods ineffective. The vulnerability affects Apple's A12 and A13 chips, and the exploit cannot be patched via software updates. This places the exploit at a high level on the Pyramid of Pain, as it requires significant effort to detect and mitigate.

diamond_model_summary: The FortiBleed campaign is a sophisticated attack attributed to Russian-speaking threat actors targeting Fortinet devices globally. The adversaries employ credential stuffing and brute-force attacks, exploiting poor password hygiene and legacy hashing mechanisms. The campaign impacts multiple sectors, including telecom, government, and education, with significant exposures in countries like India, the United States, and Mexico. The attackers have developed a bespoke tool for credential spraying, highlighting their high level of sophistication and capability.
doc_summary: The FortiBleed campaign, attributed to Russian-speaking threat actors, targets Fortinet devices globally, compromising 86,644 devices as of June 19, 2026. The attack exploits credential reuse and poor password hygiene, affecting sectors like telecom, government, and education, with significant exposures in India, the United States, Mexico, Colombia, and Thailand. The attackers use a bespoke tool for credential stuffing and brute-force attacks, leveraging older SHA-256 hashing mechanisms in FortiGate configurations. CISA and NCSC have issued advisories, urging organizations to rotate credentials and enable MFA. Fortinet has introduced PBKDF2-based hashing in newer FortiOS versions, but legacy credentials remain vulnerable. The incident highlights the importance of securing internet-facing devices and maintaining strong password policies.
kill_chain_summary: The FortiBleed campaign follows a structured kill chain, beginning with reconnaissance through mass scanning of Fortinet endpoints. The weaponization phase involves the development of a bespoke tool for credential spraying. Exploitation occurs through credential stuffing and brute-force attacks, leveraging legacy hashing mechanisms. The attackers achieve their objectives by harvesting credentials and building a verified database of working logins. The campaign demonstrates the importance of securing internet-facing devices and maintaining strong password policies.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The FortiBleed campaign presents challenges across the Pyramid of Pain, with the adversaries using legitimate credentials (TTPs) and bespoke tools for credential spraying. The attack exploits legacy hashing mechanisms, making it difficult to detect and remediate. doc_summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued a warning to Fortinet customers following the exposure of nearly 74,000 firewall and VPN credentials in a data leak known as 'FortiBleed'. Threat actors used compromised credentials to target internet-accessible Fortinet devices across government and private-sector organizations worldwide. The leak, uncovered by security researcher Volodymyr 'Bob' Diachenko, included valid Fortinet VPN credentials, usernames, email addresses, and plaintext passwords for 73,932 firewall URLs globally. The dataset also contained information on each organization's industry, revenue, and employee count. Hudson Rock described it as one of the largest known collections of compromised Fortinet credentials, spanning 21,632 unique domains and 194 countries. Notable organizations affected include Samsung, Mercedes-Benz, Foxconn, Chevron, Comcast, AT&T, and Toyota. The highest number of affected devices were from India, the United States, Taiwan, Mexico, Turkey, Thailand, Colombia, Malaysia, Chile, and the United Arab Emirates. The source of the data remains unknown, and it is unclear whether it was stolen through exploitation of previously disclosed Fortinet vulnerabilities, a newly discovered security flaw, or another method.

doc_summary: Apple has patched a high-severity vulnerability in its Beats Studio Buds wireless earbuds, tracked as CVE-2025-20701, which could be exploited by nearby hackers to eavesdrop on users. The flaw, with a CVSS score of 8.8, involves incorrect authorization in the Airoha Bluetooth audio SDK, allowing unauthorized pairing of Bluetooth audio devices. Successful exploitation could lead to remote escalation of privilege without additional execution privileges or user interaction. The issue was addressed in Beats Firmware Update 1B211. Researchers Dennis Heinze and Frieder Steinmetz from ERNW GmbH disclosed the vulnerability in June 2025, alongside two other flaws in Airoha SoCs at the TROOPERS security conference in Germany. The vulnerabilities allow attackers to take over headphones via Bluetooth, with no authentication or pairing required, and can be triggered via Bluetooth BR/EDR or BLE. Attackers can read and write the device’s RAM and flash, hijacking trust relationships with other devices.

doc_summary: Microsoft disclosed a Windows-based cryptocurrency clipper campaign targeting users since February 2026. The clipper uses Windows Script Host and ActiveX-driven logic to launch a Tor proxy and poll a hidden-service C2 server. It performs clipboard theft, screenshot exfiltration, and wallet-address substitution. The malware does not rely on traditional installers or exposed IP-based C2 infrastructure, instead using a portable Tor client and local SOCKS5 proxy. It spreads via malicious LNK files on USB devices, deploying a worm component and clipper module. The worm hides documents and creates LNK files with the same names, triggering malware execution. Persistence is achieved through scheduled tasks. The clipper uses WScript and ActiveXObject, exiting if Task Manager is running. It hijacks cryptocurrency addresses and uploads screenshots through Tor. Microsoft recommends behavioral detections, disabling AutoRun/AutoPlay, blocking LNK execution, and restricting script engines.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain involves weaponization through malicious LNK files, delivery via USB devices, installation through scheduled tasks, and command and control via Tor. Actions on objectives include clipboard theft and wallet address substitution. Detection focuses on monitoring LNK file execution, USB activity, and Tor traffic. Remediation includes disabling AutoRun/AutoPlay and restricting script engine usage.

Title: ClickFix Campaign Targeting macOS Users with Infostealer

Victim.Description: Targets include technology, media, and business services sectors in Asia, North America, and Oceania.

diamond_model_summary: The ClickFix campaign involves a Russian-speaking adversary targeting macOS users with an AppleScript-based infostealer. The attack leverages fileless execution and social engineering to deliver the payload, which is capable of harvesting credentials and maintaining persistent access. The infrastructure includes ClickFix pages masquerading as legitimate utilities, and the victims are primarily in the technology, media, and business services sectors across Asia, North America, and Oceania.
doc_summary: A Russian-speaking attacker has been observed targeting victims mainly in Asia, North America, and Oceania across technology, media, and business services sectors using ClickFix lures to deliver an AppleScript-based infostealer to macOS users. The ClickFix pages masquerade as downloads for a malware scanning utility. To evade detection, the entire infection chain, starting from the initial clipboard paste to payload execution, is completely fileless, leaving no static artifacts on disk until persistence is established. Victims are socially engineered into executing a curl command that fetches a gzip-compressed stager, which pipes the second-stage AppleScript directly into osascript memory. The second-stage, codenamed 'Meow (DEBUG),' uses a fake system dialog to harvest credentials, browser data, session cookies, and keychain contents. It's also equipped with capabilities to trojanize legitimate desktop cryptocurrency wallet applications and maintain persistent command-and-control (C2) access, allowing the operator to run arbitrary payloads.
kill_chain_summary: The ClickFix campaign follows a sophisticated kill chain involving social engineering for delivery, fileless execution for exploitation, and persistence through trojanized cryptocurrency wallets. The adversary maintains command and control via web protocols and achieves their objectives by harvesting credentials and browser data. The attack is characterized by advanced evasion techniques and a focus on macOS users.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The ClickFix campaign presents significant challenges for defenders due to its use of fileless execution and advanced evasion techniques. The lack of static artifacts makes detection difficult, and the use of legitimate tools like osascript and curl complicates attribution. The campaign's reliance on social engineering and credential harvesting further increases its impact, making it a high-severity threat.

Title: DragonForce Ransomware Incident Involving Backdoor.Turn and Microsoft Teams Infrastructure

Victim.Description: A major United States services firm targeted by DragonForce ransomware.

diamond_model_summary: The DragonForce ransomware incident involved the Hackledorb group targeting a major United States services firm. The adversary used sophisticated techniques, including the Backdoor.Turn RAT and BYOVD, to maintain persistence and evade detection. The infrastructure leveraged Microsoft's TURN relay for stealthy C2 communication, while the victim's network was compromised through an SQL vulnerability. The attack demonstrated high sophistication and persistence, marking Hackledorb as a formidable threat actor.
doc_summary: Threat actors associated with DragonForce ransomware, identified as Hackledorb, targeted a major United States services firm using a custom Go-based remote access trojan (RAT) called Backdoor.Turn. The attack leveraged Microsoft's TURN relay infrastructure to conceal command-and-control (C2) traffic. Initial access was suspected to be through an SQL or MS-SQL server vulnerability, or possibly via an initial access broker (IAB). The attack began in December 2025, involving a PowerShell command to drop a ZIP archive, leading to a DLL side-loading attack using a Huawei driver. The attackers maintained network presence for one to two months, executing Backdoor.Turn by injecting it into the DbgView64.exe process. The backdoor facilitated command execution, process creation, network scanning, and credential theft. The incident marks the first documented abuse of Microsoft's TURN relay infrastructure by threat actors.

Delivery was executed via PowerShell, leading to exploitation of an SQL vulnerability for initial access. Installation involved DLL side-loading to deploy Backdoor.Turn, which facilitated command and control through Microsoft's TURN relay infrastructure. Actions on objectives included credential theft and lateral movement, highlighting the attack's complexity and stealth.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves critical vulnerabilities in NGINX web server products, which could be exploited by remote attackers to execute code or cause denial-of-service attacks. F5 has released security updates to mitigate these vulnerabilities. The adversary's identity and motivation remain unknown, but the potential impact is significant due to the widespread use of NGINX products.
doc_summary: F5, a Fortune 500 technology company, released out-of-band security updates to address multiple vulnerabilities in NGINX web server products, including two critical-severity flaws in the ngx_http_v3_module and ngx_http_proxy_v2_module. These vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-42530 and CVE-2026-42055, could allow unauthenticated remote attackers to execute code or trigger denial-of-service attacks on systems with non-default configurations. Successful exploitation may lead to use-after-free or heap-based buffer overflow in the NGINX worker process. F5 provided security fixes for NGINX Plus, NGINX Open Source, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and NGINX Instance Manager. Mitigation steps include disabling HTTP/3 and adjusting configuration directives. Although no active exploitation was reported, F5 vulnerabilities have been targeted by cybercrime and nation-state groups. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has noted F5 products in ransomware attacks. F5 serves over 23,000 customers, including major Fortune companies.

Victim.Description: Federal agencies and other organizations using vulnerable Joomla JCE plugin.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves the exploitation of a critical vulnerability in the Widget Factory Joomla Content Editor plugin. The adversary is leveraging improper access control to execute unauthorized PHP code. The infrastructure targeted includes Joomla deployments using the vulnerable plugin. Victims are primarily federal agencies in the United States, with the potential for broader impact due to the public availability of exploit code.
doc_summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has mandated federal agencies to patch a critical vulnerability in the Widget Factory Joomla Content Editor (JCE) plugin. This flaw, actively exploited in the wild, allows unauthorized code execution via low-complexity attacks. The vulnerability stems from improper access control, enabling PHP code upload and execution through new editor profiles for unauthenticated users. The JCE security team released a patch in early June, urging immediate updates due to public exploit code and automated attacks. CISA's Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04 requires federal agencies to secure systems by Friday, emphasizing the risk posed by this frequent attack vector. Agencies must evaluate internet exposure and adhere to patching guidelines. The directive highlights the importance of patching based on exploitation risk, public exposure, automation potential, and control level granted to attackers.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with the exploitation of a public-facing application vulnerability in the Joomla JCE plugin, allowing unauthorized code execution. The exploitation stage is critical, as it enables the adversary to gain initial access without authentication. Detection focuses on monitoring unauthorized profile creation and PHP uploads. Remediation involves patching the plugin and conducting thorough malware scans.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident is primarily focused on the TTPs, as the exploitation of the Joomla JCE plugin vulnerability is a key tactic. Detection efforts should prioritize identifying unauthorized profile creation and PHP uploads. The public availability of exploit code increases the challenge of mitigation, emphasizing the need for timely patching and comprehensive security measures.

Title: Compromise of Mastra npm Packages via easy-day-js Supply Chain Attack

Victim.Description: The victims are users of the Mastra npm packages, particularly those in AI and cloud infrastructure sectors.

diamond_model_summary: The attack on the Mastra npm packages involved an adversary who hijacked the 'ehindero' account to publish malicious packages. The capability included the use of a cloned library 'easy-day-js' to deliver a cryptocurrency-stealing trojan. The infrastructure involved C2 servers for payload delivery and data exfiltration. Victims were users of the Mastra packages, particularly in AI and cloud infrastructure sectors.
doc_summary: In June 2026, a significant supply chain attack targeted the Mastra namespace on npm, compromising 144 packages. The attack involved the insertion of a malicious dependency, 'easy-day-js', which acted as a dropper for a cryptocurrency-stealing trojan. The attack was executed by hijacking the npm account 'ehindero', a former Mastra contributor. The malicious package was published by 'sergey2016' and introduced a payload that disabled TLS certificate validation and communicated with C2 servers at '23.254.164.92' and '23.254.164.123'. The attack leveraged Mastra's position in AI and cloud infrastructure, making it a high-value target. The campaign demonstrated advanced techniques, including obfuscated payloads, persistence mechanisms, and cross-platform data exfiltration capabilities. The incident highlighted vulnerabilities in npm's publishing process and the need for stronger provenance and signature verification.
kill_chain_summary: The attack followed a structured kill chain, starting with reconnaissance to identify the Mastra namespace as a target. Weaponization involved cloning the 'dayjs' library to create 'easy-day-js'. Delivery was achieved through npm as a dependency. Exploitation occurred during the npm installation process. Installation involved a background process with persistence. Command and control were maintained via C2 servers. Actions on objectives included stealing cryptocurrency wallet data.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes IP addresses of C2 servers, the 'easy-day-js' tool, and TTPs such as supply chain attacks and obfuscated payload delivery. These indicators are critical for detection and response efforts. The attack demonstrated advanced techniques, making it challenging to detect and mitigate. The use of hijacked accounts and cloned libraries highlights the need for robust security measures in software supply chains.

Title: Exploitation of CVE-2026-48907 in Joomla Content Editor

Victim.Description: Websites using vulnerable Joomla JCE versions.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a Turkish-speaking threat actor exploiting a critical vulnerability in the Joomla Content Editor (CVE-2026-48907) to execute arbitrary PHP code. The adversary's capability includes exploiting improper access controls to upload malicious code. The infrastructure targeted includes websites using vulnerable Joomla versions, primarily in the technology sector in the United States. The victim's assets at risk include web servers and content management systems, with a high impact severity due to the potential for widespread exploitation.
doc_summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added a critical security flaw impacting Widget Factory Joomla Content Editor (JCE) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The vulnerability, CVE-2026-48907, allows improper access control leading to arbitrary code execution. It affects JCE versions 1.0.0 through 2.9.99.4 and is patched in version 2.9.99.5. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies must apply fixes by June 19, 2026. Concurrently, Sansec detailed a supply chain attack on WordPress plugins, with threat actors injecting malicious JavaScript to create backdoor admin accounts. A separate campaign involved a fake WordPress plugin, 'Beloved PBN Entegrasyonu', used for SEO monetization by a Turkish-speaking actor.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with the exploitation of a public-facing application vulnerability (CVE-2026-48907) in Joomla Content Editor, allowing the adversary to gain initial access. The installation phase involves deploying backdoor plugins and PHP web shells to maintain persistence. Actions on objectives include SEO manipulation through backlink injection, damaging search rankings. Detection focuses on monitoring PHP uploads and unauthorized plugin installations, while remediation involves applying patches and removing unauthorized changes.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes the exploitation of CVE-2026-48907, a critical vulnerability in Joomla Content Editor, as a TTP. The adversary's use of PHP code execution and unauthorized plugin installations are key indicators. The lack of specific hash values, IP addresses, or domain names limits the ability to track the adversary's infrastructure. The focus is on detecting unusual PHP uploads and unauthorized changes to web applications.

Title: Malicious Plugins on JetBrains Marketplace Steal AI API Keys

Victim.Description: Developers using the JetBrains Marketplace plugins are targeted.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a coordinated malware campaign targeting developers using the JetBrains Marketplace. The adversary's capability includes developing malicious plugins that exfiltrate AI API keys. The infrastructure involves a hardcoded server for data exfiltration. Victims are developers in the software development industry.
doc_summary: Aikido Security discovered a coordinated malware campaign on the JetBrains Marketplace involving at least 15 malicious plugins designed to steal AI API keys from developers. These plugins, acting as AI coding assistants and code-review tools, were published under seven vendor accounts and have been installed nearly 70,000 times. The plugins exfiltrate API keys to a hardcoded server at 39.107.60.51 over HTTP. The campaign began in October 2025, with new plugins published as recently as June 10, 2026. The plugins also offer a paid tier, providing harvested API keys to paying users. BleepingComputer confirmed the presence of credential theft code in the DeepSeek AI Assist plugin. JetBrains has not responded to inquiries about the incident.
kill_chain_summary: The attack follows a structured kill chain: reconnaissance to identify targets, weaponization of plugins, delivery through the JetBrains Marketplace, exploitation upon installation, installation of malicious code, command and control via exfiltration to a remote server, and actions on objectives by stealing and potentially reselling API keys.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes IP addresses and tools as key indicators. The IP address 39.107.60.51 is used for exfiltration, and malicious IDE plugins serve as tools. These indicators are crucial for detection and response efforts, highlighting the adversary's reliance on specific infrastructure and tools.

Title: Malware Distribution via Steam Workshop Wallpaper Engine

Victim.Description: Steam users downloading malicious wallpapers.
Victim.Security_Posture: Vulnerable due to lack of awareness and security measures.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves threat actors exploiting Steam Workshop to distribute malware via Wallpaper Engine. The adversaries are financially motivated, using the platform's vulnerabilities to hijack accounts, install backdoors, and run cryptomining processes. The infrastructure includes the Steam Workshop, and victims are global Steam users.
doc_summary: Threat actors are exploiting Steam Workshop, a platform for game-related content, to distribute malware through wallpaper packages. These malicious wallpapers can hijack Steam accounts, install backdoors like DarkKomet, and run cryptomining processes. Kaspersky researchers identified the abuse of Wallpaper Engine, which supports executable Windows applications as wallpapers. Malicious files are either bundled directly or hidden in password-protected archives. The malware includes infostealers like Lumma and Vidar, botnet loaders, and ransomware. Despite Valve's removal of identified threats, new submissions are likely. Users are advised to download from trusted sources and use up-to-date antivirus software.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with reconnaissance to identify vulnerabilities in Steam Workshop and Wallpaper Engine. Weaponization involves creating malicious wallpaper packages. Delivery occurs through uploading these packages to Steam Workshop. Exploitation leverages Wallpaper Engine's ability to run executables. Installation involves malware like DarkKomet. Command and Control is established for system control, and actions on objectives include account hijacking and cryptomining.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes malware families like DarkKomet, Lumma, and Vidar. The use of Wallpaper Engine as a tool for malware distribution is significant. No specific IP addresses or domains were identified, but the exploitation of Steam Workshop is a key network host artifact. The TTPs involve malware distribution and credential theft.

doc_summary: Rokarolla is a new Android banking trojan targeting 217 banking and cryptocurrency applications. Distributed via malicious websites, it impersonates Google Play Protect and requests accessibility service permissions. The malware communicates with a command-and-control server, sending device profiles to generate unique identifiers for victims. Rokarolla's primary objective is financial data theft, using phishing overlays to steal credentials and credit card information. It employs evasion tactics like disabling Google Play Protect and hiding its icon. Zimperium researchers highlight its extensive command set and administrative control capabilities.
kill_chain_summary: The Rokarolla malware follows a structured kill chain, starting with delivery via malicious websites. diamond_model_summary: The ClickFix campaigns involve adversaries using social engineering to deliver modular loaders like BabaDeda, Lorem Ipsum, and Potemkin. These loaders target sectors such as education, financial, architecture, and legal, employing advanced evasion techniques and modular frameworks for stealthy malware delivery and execution.
doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers have identified multiple ClickFix campaigns delivering malware loaders BabaDeda, Lorem Ipsum, and Potemkin. BabaDeda Loader targets education and financial sectors, using PowerShell commands and evasion techniques to avoid Russian and Belarusian systems. Lorem Ipsum Loader, linked to Vanilla Tempest, exploits compromised WordPress sites in architecture and legal services. Potemkin Loader, detected by Huntress, uses MSI packages and HTA payloads for EtherRAT deployment. These campaigns demonstrate adaptability in malware delivery, leveraging social engineering and modular loader frameworks. The campaigns highlight the ongoing threat posed by actors like Vanilla Tempest and the impact of Microsoft's disruption of Fox Tempest's malware-signing services.
kill_chain_summary: The ClickFix campaigns follow a structured kill chain, starting with reconnaissance of vulnerable WordPress sites, weaponization of modular loaders, and delivery via social engineering. Exploitation involves user trust manipulation, leading to installation of loaders and malware components. Command and control is established through C2 channels, culminating in actions on objectives like data theft and ransomware deployment.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The ClickFix campaigns present challenges across the Pyramid of Pain, with adversaries using modular loaders and advanced evasion techniques. Hash values, IP addresses, and domain names are less impactful, while tools like PowerShell and Node.js, along with TTPs such as social engineering and DLL side-loading, pose significant challenges for detection and response.

Title: Pickle in the Middle: Google Cloud Vertex AI SDK Vulnerability

Victim.Description: Victims were users of the Google Cloud Vertex AI SDK who did not set explicit bucket names.
Victim.Security_Posture: Vulnerable due to default SDK settings

diamond_model_summary: The incident involved an adversary exploiting a vulnerability in the Google Cloud Vertex AI SDK to hijack machine learning model uploads. The adversary used predictable bucket names to intercept and replace model uploads, leveraging Google Cloud infrastructure. Victims were users of the SDK who did not set explicit bucket names, leading to unauthorized access to model artifacts and OAuth tokens.
doc_summary: A vulnerability in the Google Cloud Vertex AI SDK for Python allowed attackers to hijack machine learning model uploads without access to the victim's project. Discovered by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, the flaw, dubbed 'Pickle in the Middle', involved predictable bucket names in Google Cloud Storage. Attackers could create a bucket with the expected name, intercepting model uploads and replacing them with malicious ones. Users are advised to update the SDK and set explicit bucket names.

doc_summary: Security researchers at Zimperium's zLabs have identified a new Android banking trojan named Rokarolla. This malware targets 217 banking and cryptocurrency apps, utilizing 137 remote commands to gain control over infected devices. Rokarolla spreads through malicious websites masquerading as popular apps like TikTok and Chrome. Rokarolla employs HTML overlays to capture credentials by mimicking legitimate banking app login pages. It also reads and sends SMS, intercepts one-time codes, and rewrites clipboard contents to redirect cryptocurrency payments. Zimperium's products can detect Rokarolla, and indicators of compromise are available in their GitHub repository.

doc_summary: A critical vulnerability in SimpleHelp remote management software allows unauthenticated attackers to create privileged technician accounts using the OpenID Connect (OIDC) authentication protocol. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-48558, affects SimpleHelp versions 5.5.15 and older, as well as 6.0 pre-release versions. Horizon3.ai researchers identified the issue, which is caused by improper validation of identity assertions from an OIDC identity provider. The vulnerability enables attackers to bypass multi-factor authentication and perform privileged management activities. Approximately 14,000 SimpleHelp servers are exposed to the internet, with 7.2% configured to use OIDC authentication. Organizations are advised to update to the latest SimpleHelp releases or restrict technician login sources using IP-based allowlists. Indicators of compromise include new technician users with suspicious names or email addresses and rogue account activities in server logs.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain for this incident involves exploiting a vulnerability in SimpleHelp's OIDC authentication process. The adversary can bypass authentication controls to create privileged technician accounts, allowing them to perform unauthorized actions on affected servers. The exploitation stage is critical, as it enables the adversary to gain access without multi-factor authentication. The actions on objectives stage involves using these accounts to perform privileged management activities, potentially impacting the integrity and availability of the victim's systems. Detection involves monitoring for suspicious account creation and management activities, while remediation includes updating to patched versions and restricting login sources.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident is primarily focused on the TTPs used by the adversary, specifically the exploitation of the CVE-2026-48558 vulnerability in SimpleHelp's OIDC authentication process. No specific hash values, IP addresses, or domain names are identified, but the use of OIDC as a communication protocol is a key indicator. The tools and techniques employed by the adversary are critical to understanding and mitigating the threat. Organizations should focus on detecting unauthorized account creation and management activities as indicators of compromise. Remediation efforts should prioritize patching vulnerable systems and implementing IP-based allowlists.

doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers have identified a phishing campaign, UNK_DeadDrop, linked to North Korean threat actors, targeting nearly 100 organizations across finance, cryptocurrency, education, and technology sectors. The campaign uses phishing emails with links to GitHub repositories hosting malicious scripts, leading to the execution of cross-platform malware for macOS, Linux, and Windows. The malware includes a custom version of the Overlord framework, designed to steal credentials and data from wallet browser extensions and applications. The campaign is notable for its use of Microsoft Visual Studio Code projects to execute malicious code without user interaction. The activity has been observed primarily in the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, France, Brazil, Germany, India, Israel, Japan, and the Netherlands. The campaign's infrastructure includes a command and control server at 23.137.105.75:5173. The threat actor's tactics have evolved from social engineering on social media to large-scale phishing campaigns, indicating a maturation of North Korean cyber operations.
kill_chain_summary: The UNK_DeadDrop campaign follows a structured kill chain, beginning with reconnaissance through phishing emails targeting developers. Weaponization involves the creation of malicious scripts hosted on GitHub repositories. Delivery is achieved via phishing emails containing links to these repositories. Exploitation occurs through the execution of malicious code in Microsoft Visual Studio Code. Installation involves the deployment of malicious VS Code extensions. Command and control is established through communication with a C2 server at 23.137.105.75:5173. Finally, actions on objectives include data exfiltration from wallet extensions and applications.

The vulnerabilities are rated CVSS 9.9, and a fix is available in LiteLLM v1.83.14-stable. The proxy's position makes it a target, with risks including data leakage and response manipulation. Obsidian demonstrated a reverse shell exploit using LiteLLM's callback mechanism. The incident highlights the importance of upgrading to the patched version and auditing proxy admin accounts and configurations.

Title: FBI Warns of Cryptocurrency Investment Scam Using Couriers

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves criminals using social engineering to lure victims into cryptocurrency investment scams. The adversaries employ couriers to collect cash from victims, using agreed-upon passwords or dollar bill serial numbers for authentication. The infrastructure includes social media, dating sites, and messaging apps for initial contact. Victims are individuals in the United States, targeted for their cryptocurrency funds. The adversaries' motivation is financial gain, and the impact severity is high due to significant financial losses.
doc_summary: The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) issued a warning about criminals using couriers to collect money from victims of cryptocurrency investment scams. These scams typically begin with fraudsters contacting targets via social media, dating sites, and messaging apps, building trust, and then luring victims into fake investment schemes. Instead of investing funds, scammers steal the money by transferring it into accounts they control. The FBI's public service announcement highlighted that scammers are pushing victims toward in-person cash pickups after legitimate financial institutions block suspicious money transfers. Couriers identify themselves using an agreed-upon password or a specific dollar bill serial number. Victims see a simulated increase in their virtual wallet balance and attempt to withdraw winnings, but scammers restart the cycle, demanding more cash for fraudulent taxes and penalties. The FBI advised researching cryptocurrency platforms before investing, not sharing home addresses, and stopping contact after unsolicited communications. Victims are urged to report incidents with as much information as possible. The FBI noted that U.S. victims lost nearly $21 billion to cyber-enabled crimes last year, with investment scams accounting for 49% of incidents and $8.6 billion in losses.

Title: China-linked Espionage Campaign Targets REDCap Servers with InfiniteRed Malware

Victim.Description: A medical institution in North America using REDCap servers was targeted.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a China-linked threat actor, UNC6508, targeting REDCap servers in North America. The adversary deployed the InfiniteRed malware, which includes a persistence module, credential harvester, and backdoor. The infrastructure used includes US-based residential proxies and compromised routers. The victim is a medical institution in North America, with sensitive medical research data at risk. The campaign demonstrates high operational security and advanced tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
doc_summary: A China-linked espionage campaign targeted exposed REDCap servers to deploy the InfiniteRed malware and steal sensitive data from a medical institution in North America. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) researchers attribute the attacks to a threat actor tracked as UNC6508, who remained undetected for more than a year in the victim network. The REDCap platform is widely used in medical and scientific research to build and manage databases and surveys that comply with regulations for medical and scientific research. Although the researchers couldn’t determine the exact initial compromise vector, they observed UNC6508 probing older, vulnerable versions of REDCap. Based on the investigation, the compromise of the medical research organization occurred in September 2023, and the malicious activity continued for more than a year through November 2025. Three months after the initial compromise, the attackers deployed the 'InfiniteRed' custom malware designed specifically for REDCap systems, and hid its components by trojanizing the server’s system files. InfiniteRed consists of three components: a persistence/update module, a credential harvester, and a backdoor. The login harvester captures usernames and passwords submitted through REDCap login pages, then encrypts and stores them in local REDCap database tables for future retrieval. The backdoor, which receives commands via HTTP cookies, provides UNC6508 with the following abilities: One notable technique in the campaign, and new for China-linked threat actors, is the use of the legitimate 'content compliance rules' feature that is present in cloud-based enterprise productivity tools, to exfiltrate data over email. After gaining administrator access, UNC6508 created a content compliance rule named “Patroit,” which scans the organization for specific keywords, content patterns, email addresses, and phone numbers. Any matches are then automatically sent as a blind carbon copy (BCC) to ‘BebitaBarefoot774@gmail.com,’ now disabled by Google. The keywords used to look for data of value relate to medical research, advanced technology, military topics, and geo-strategic policy. GTIG observed a high level of operational security across this campaign, including the use of US-based residential proxy infrastructure, compromised routers, VPS, credential replay, and dedicated infrastructure for data exfiltration. Google notified multiple organizations in the United States and Canada that were compromised with the InfiniteRed malware. Their research areas span a broad spectrum of modern medicine, from molecular discovery and clinical drug trials to state-level public health policy and military readiness. REDCap administrators are recommended to upgrade their instances to the latest available versions and remove legacy deployments. Google also advises using MFA/2SV on high-privilege accounts and Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) to prevent session hijacking. YARA rules and indicators of compromise (IoCs) are present in the report to help scan environments for InfiniteRed malware infections.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain begins with reconnaissance, where UNC6508 probed vulnerable REDCap versions. Weaponization involved developing the InfiniteRed malware. Exploitation occurred through vulnerable REDCap servers, followed by installation of the malware. Command and control were maintained via HTTP cookies. Actions on objectives included data exfiltration using content compliance rules. The campaign highlights advanced tactics and operational security.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes the InfiniteRed malware hash values, the use of HTTP cookies for command and control, and the exploitation of REDCap vulnerabilities. The adversary's use of legitimate features for data exfiltration adds complexity to detection and response efforts. The campaign demonstrates a high level of sophistication and operational security, making it challenging to disrupt.

Title: Cyber Av3ngers Exploit Default Credentials in Aliquippa Water Authority Attack

Victim.Description: Municipal Water Authority of Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, United States.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involving the Municipal Water Authority of Aliquippa highlights the exploitation of default credentials by the Iranian-linked hacktivist group Cyber Av3ngers. The adversary leveraged default PLC credentials to gain unauthorized access to a remote booster station. doc_summary: In November 2023, the Municipal Water Authority of Aliquippa in Pennsylvania, United States, was targeted by the Iranian-linked hacktivist group Cyber Av3ngers. The attackers exploited programmable logic controllers (PLCs) protected by the default credential '1111', allowing them to gain control of a remote booster station serving two townships. Although there was no risk to the water supply, the incident highlighted the severity of using default credentials in operational technology environments. CISA issued alerts to other facilities to update default credentials and disconnect PLCs from the open internet. This incident underscores the risks associated with unchanged default or temporary credentials, particularly when exposed on internet-facing systems.
kill_chain_summary: The attack on the Municipal Water Authority of Aliquippa followed a clear kill chain involving the exploitation of default credentials in PLCs. The adversary, Cyber Av3ngers, used these credentials to gain unauthorized access to a remote booster station, demonstrating the critical need for securing default credentials and implementing network segmentation to protect critical infrastructure.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain analysis for this incident reveals the critical impact of default credentials as a TTP. The adversary exploited these credentials to gain unauthorized access to critical infrastructure, highlighting the need for organizations to prioritize the updating of default credentials and the implementation of network segmentation to mitigate such risks.

Title: Malicious Chrome Extensions Distributing Adware and Traffic Fraud

Victim.Description: Users of Google Chrome who installed the malicious extensions.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a network of malicious Chrome extensions used for adware distribution and traffic fraud. The adversary is financially motivated, potentially originating from Turkey, and employs Chrome extensions to manipulate traffic signals and collect user data. The infrastructure includes multiple Chrome Web Store accounts and backend domains. Victims are global users of Google Chrome who installed these extensions.
doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers have identified a network of 152 Google Chrome extensions acting as new tab live wallpaper add-ons to distribute a potentially unwanted program (PUP) family. These extensions span 38 separate Chrome Web Store publisher accounts and three brand backends: tabplugins.com, yowgames.com, and chromewallpaper.com, collectively installed 105,000 times. Despite claims of not collecting user data, the extensions log IP addresses, ISP, click counts, and referrers, sharing data with Google AdSense, DoubleClick, and third-party ad partners. A sub-cluster of extensions defines two hard-coded URLs in a JavaScript file activated during install and uninstall operations, fabricating traffic origin signals. The campaign is assessed as a financially motivated commercial adware and traffic-attribution-fraud affiliate operation, potentially originating from Turkey.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with reconnaissance of Chrome Web Store policies, followed by weaponization through the development of malicious extensions. Delivery occurs via the Chrome Web Store, exploiting user trust to install the extensions. Once installed, the extensions collect data and manipulate traffic signals, communicating with backend servers for data exfiltration. The final objective is adware distribution and traffic fraud.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes domain names such as tabplugins.com, yowgames.com, and chromewallpaper.com, which are critical for the operation of the malicious extensions. The extensions themselves act as tools for adware distribution and traffic fraud. No specific IP addresses or file hashes were identified, limiting the ability to disrupt the adversary's operations.

doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers from Group-IB disclosed a phishing campaign targeting users in the Middle East and North Africa. The campaign used fraudulent Facebook accounts impersonating politicians and organizations to promote fake offers. Victims were redirected through intermediary websites to phishing and traffic monetization infrastructure. The campaign was linked to Sniper Dz, a phishing-as-a-service platform dismantled by INTERPOL. Techniques included browser notification abuse, premium SMS subscriptions, and investment scams. The campaign exploited trusted platforms like Linkbio and Linktree, using VAPID keys for push notifications. The attack involved social engineering, history manipulation, and tab-under techniques to trap users and monetize traffic.

Weaponization involved creating fraudulent accounts and phishing pages. Delivery was executed via social media posts with malicious links. The campaign demonstrated a sophisticated use of social engineering and legitimate web technologies to achieve its objectives.

Title: Dismantling of Outsider Enterprise Phishing Operation

Victim.Description: Victims include Android users receiving phishing SMS messages.

diamond_model_summary: The Outsider Enterprise operation represents a sophisticated phishing-as-a-service model, leveraging AI and a vast infrastructure of fake websites to impersonate trusted brands. The adversary, based in China, targeted global users, primarily through SMS phishing, resulting in significant financial losses. The operation's infrastructure included thousands of domains and a Telegram bot for coordination.
doc_summary: The FBI, in collaboration with Google and Black Lotus Labs, dismantled a large-scale Chinese phishing-as-a-service operation known as Outsider Enterprise. This operation involved thousands of phishing websites and AI-assisted phishing kits impersonating trusted brands via SMS through AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon. Active since at least 2023, Outsider Enterprise was linked to 9,000 fake websites and over a million fraudulent URLs, resulting in the theft of more than 3.8 million credit card records and $1.9 billion in losses. The FBI's Operation Riptide seized multiple servers, a Shopify storefront, and a Telegram bot associated with the operation. Google filed a civil lawsuit targeting the infrastructure and is working with telecom providers to block fraudulent messages. The Stop SCAMS Act is proposed to enhance anti-scam strategies in the United States.
kill_chain_summary: The Outsider Enterprise operation followed a structured kill chain, beginning with reconnaissance to identify targets, followed by weaponization through the development of phishing kits. Delivery was executed via SMS, leading to exploitation through user interaction with phishing links. The operation's objectives were achieved through the collection and use of stolen data for financial gain.

doc_summary: Ezekiel Dean Potter, a former IT employee at Saydel Community School District in Iowa, conducted a prolonged cyberattack against his former employer. The attack disrupted classroom operations, deleted accounts, and caused significant financial damage. Potter retained access credentials after his employment ended and targeted the district's systems over 21 months. He deleted the district's Facebook page, stripped employees of access to educational platforms, and attempted to reset usernames and passwords. The attacks impaired the district's ability to teach and resulted in tens of thousands of dollars in remediation costs. Potter accessed the district's Apple School Manager account, deleting user accounts and device management data, which disabled management of district MacBooks and iPads. Unauthorized access attempts were also made against the district's GoDaddy account and other services. Potter used a VPN service to evade detection, but federal investigators traced activity to IP addresses associated with his other employers. He pleaded guilty to computer fraud charges and was sentenced to 21 months in prison, with restitution required.
kill_chain_summary: The attack began with Potter retaining access credentials after his employment ended, allowing him to conduct reconnaissance. He exploited these credentials to access systems and used VPN services to evade detection. Potter's actions on objectives included deleting accounts and disrupting operations, causing significant impact on the school district.
